concepts.name: A human review queue with confidence thresholds
An audit trail for every decision

questions.prompt: About 5,000 invoices arrive by email each day, and accounting needs the extracted fields in the CRM by the next morning. Which processing mode fits best?

choices.text: Real time, because batch processing gives less accurate extractions
Batch, because nobody waits for each result and batch APIs cost less
Real time, because batch APIs only accept a few hundred requests at once
Batch, because real-time APIs can't read PDF documents

questions.explanation: The deadline is hours away and no user is waiting, which is exactly what batch APIs are for. Anthropic's Message Batches API charges 50% of standard prices, takes up to 100,000 requests per batch, and finishes most batches within an hour (at most 24 hours). The model and accuracy are the same either way.

sources.title: Batch processing
sources.claim: The Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously at 50% of standard prices, accepts up to 100,000 requests (or 256 MB) per batch, and finishes most batches within an hour, expiring any not done within 24 hours.

questions.prompt: Which requirement forces the pipeline to have a real-time path?

choices.text: Month-end reports built from all documents processed that month
Re-processing last year's archive with a new prompt
A user uploads a document in the app and waits to check the extracted fields
A nightly reconciliation of the CRM against the document store

questions.explanation: A person waiting on screen needs an answer in seconds, and a batch job can take up to 24 hours. Reports, backfills and nightly reconciliation all tolerate delay, so they can use the cheaper batch path. Many pipelines run both: real time for interactive uploads, batch for everything else.

sources.title: Batch processing
sources.claim: Batch processing suits work that does not need an immediate response; results can take up to 24 hours, so an interactive user waiting on screen needs the standard real-time Messages API.

questions.prompt: Workers read document jobs from an SQS queue that uses the default visibility timeout of 30 seconds. Each document takes about 3 minutes to process. What happens?

choices.text: Each job reappears after 30 seconds and another worker processes the same document
SQS extends the timeout automatically while a worker is still busy with the message
SQS deletes the message after 30 seconds unprocessed, so the document is lost for good
Nothing: the visibility timeout only applies to FIFO queues, not standard ones

questions.explanation: A received message stays in the queue but is hidden for the visibility timeout. If it isn't deleted in time, it becomes visible again and another consumer can take it, so slow jobs get processed several times. Set the timeout above your processing time, or extend it with `ChangeMessageVisibility` as a heartbeat. Even then SQS delivers at least once, so processing must be idempotent.

sources.title: Amazon SQS visibility timeout
sources.claim: A received message stays in the queue hidden for the visibility timeout (default 30 seconds); if not deleted before it expires it becomes visible again for another consumer, the timeout can be extended with ChangeMessageVisibility, and at-least-once delivery means duplicates are still possible.

questions.prompt: A corrupt PDF crashes the extractor every time. The queue has a redrive policy with `maxReceiveCount` set to 5 and a dead-letter queue. What happens to that message?

choices.text: SQS deletes it after the fifth failure
After it has been received 5 times without being deleted, SQS moves it to the dead-letter queue
It's retried forever, because the redrive policy only applies to FIFO queues
It moves to the dead-letter queue on its very first failure

questions.explanation: `maxReceiveCount` is how many times a message can be received before SQS moves it to the dead-letter queue. That stops a poison message from cycling forever and lets you inspect it. Set an alarm on the dead-letter queue, and set its retention longer than the source queue's, because a standard queue message keeps its original enqueue time.

sources.title: Using dead-letter queues in Amazon SQS
sources.claim: maxReceiveCount in the redrive policy is how many times a message can be received from the source queue before SQS moves it to the dead-letter queue, and for standard queues the DLQ retention should exceed the source's because the original enqueue timestamp is kept.

questions.prompt: Why must the step that pushes an approved record to the CRM be idempotent?

choices.text: Idempotent calls are faster, which keeps the queue short and the reviewers unblocked
Most CRM APIs reject any write request that isn't marked with an idempotency header
It only matters with a FIFO queue, since standard queues never deliver a message twice
Retries and at-least-once delivery can repeat it; an idempotency key stops duplicate records

questions.explanation: A timeout after the CRM accepted the write, a redelivered queue message, or a resumed workflow can all repeat the step. LangGraph, for example, re-runs a node from its start when resuming after an `interrupt`. Send a key that identifies the operation (such as document ID plus version), so the API recognises a retry: Stripe's API saves the first result for a key and returns it for repeats.

sources.title: Idempotent requests
sources.claim: Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request made with an idempotency key and returns that same result for later requests with the key, so a retry cannot create a second object.

sources.title: Amazon SQS visibility timeout
sources.claim: Because of SQS's at-least-once delivery model, a message can be delivered more than once, including on standard queues, so consumers must tolerate repeats.

sources.title: Interrupts
sources.claim: interrupt() needs a checkpointer and a thread_id in the config, execution resumes by invoking the graph with Command(resume=...), and on resume the node restarts from its beginning so code before interrupt runs again.

questions.prompt: Design the retry policy for the pipeline's LLM extraction step. Which failures do you retry, how, and what happens when retries run out?

model_answer.summary: Retry transient failures with capped exponential backoff and jitter, retry validation failures a few times with the error fed back, never retry permanent errors blindly, and send anything still failing to a dead-letter or review queue.
key_points: Transient errors (rate limits, 5xx responses, timeouts) are retried with exponential backoff plus jitter, such as tenacity's `wait_random_exponential`
Attempts are capped, for example with `stop_after_attempt`, so a failing document can't retry forever
Output that fails schema or business-rule validation is retried a small number of times with the validation error included in the prompt
Permanent errors, such as an unreadable file, are not retried; they go straight to the dead-letter or human review queue
Downstream writes are idempotent, so a retry never creates a duplicate record

questions.explanation: Retrying everything wastes money and can make an overloaded provider worse; retrying nothing loses documents to brief glitches. Jitter spreads retries out so many workers don't retry in step. Retries only become safe once the side effects are idempotent.

sources.title: Tenacity
sources.claim: Tenacity provides wait_random_exponential for randomised exponential backoff, stop_after_attempt to cap the number of attempts, and retry_if_exception_type to retry only chosen exception types.

sources.title: Retry behavior
sources.claim: AWS SDKs retry only transient and throttling errors, using exponential backoff with full jitter so clients don't retry in step, cap total attempts (default 3), and return non-retryable errors such as validation failures immediately.

sources.title: Retrying
sources.claim: With max_retries set, Instructor retries when Pydantic validation fails and feeds the validation error back to the model so it can correct its output.

questions.prompt: Documents above a confidence threshold are approved automatically; the rest go to human review. How should you choose the threshold?

choices.text: Use 0.9, since it's the standard threshold for document extraction and keeps errors under 1%
Ask the model to rate its own confidence and auto-approve anything it rates above 0.8
On labelled data, measure errors and review volume at each threshold; pick one that meets your error target
Send everything to review until the model has processed 10,000 documents, then auto-approve all

questions.explanation: A threshold is a trade-off between errors that slip through and reviewer workload, and only labelled data shows where that trade-off sits for your documents. A model's self-rated confidence isn't guaranteed to match its real accuracy, so treat it as one signal to test, not a fact. Combine it with deterministic checks (schema validation, totals that add up) and re-check the threshold as documents change.

sources.title: Thresholds and the confusion matrix
sources.claim: There is no universal classification threshold: raising it trades false positives for false negatives, so the threshold should be chosen by measuring outcomes on labelled data against the relative cost of each error type.

sources.title: Using Amazon Augmented AI for Human Review
sources.claim: Amazon A2I routes low-confidence predictions (for example Textract document extractions) to human reviewers and can also send a random sample of predictions for review to audit the model on an ongoing basis.

questions.prompt: Why also send a small random sample of auto-approved documents to human review?

choices.text: To measure the otherwise invisible error rate of the automatic path and spot drift
To keep reviewers busy and practised when the main review queue is running empty
Because data regulations require every automated decision to be reviewed twice by humans
To collect labels and fine-tune the model online on every document a reviewer checks

questions.explanation: Errors in auto-approved documents never reach a reviewer, so without sampling you can't know how often the threshold lets mistakes through, or notice when new document layouts make it worse. This is the pipeline version of applied-llms.org's advice to look at samples of real inputs and outputs every day.

sources.title: Using Amazon Augmented AI for Human Review
sources.claim: Amazon A2I routes low-confidence predictions (for example Textract document extractions) to human reviewers and can also send a random sample of predictions for review to audit the model on an ongoing basis.

questions.prompt: Design the human review queue for project 2: what gets routed there, what reviewers see, and how their decisions flow back into the pipeline.

model_answer.summary: Documents that fail a threshold, a validation check or a business rule are paused and queued; reviewers see the source next to the extracted fields with problems highlighted; their decision resumes the pipeline and their corrections become eval data.
key_points: Routing rules: confidence below the threshold, schema or business-rule failures, or high-impact cases such as amounts above a limit, plus a random sample of auto-approved documents
The pipeline pauses and saves its state while waiting, for example with LangGraph's `interrupt`, which needs a checkpointer and a thread ID
Reviewers see the original document beside the extracted fields, with the flagged fields and the reason highlighted
The reviewer approves, edits or rejects; the decision is passed back (in LangGraph, with `Command(resume=...)`) and the pipeline continues
Every correction is recorded and added to the eval set, so the prompt and threshold can improve

questions.explanation: A review queue is only useful if pausing is durable (the process may restart while a document waits for days) and if decisions are captured. LangGraph re-runs the interrupted node from its start on resume, so code before the `interrupt` call must be safe to repeat.

sources.title: Interrupts
sources.claim: interrupt() needs a checkpointer and a thread_id in the config, execution resumes by invoking the graph with Command(resume=...), and on resume the node restarts from its beginning so code before interrupt runs again.

questions.prompt: Six months from now someone asks why a particular CRM record has the values it has. What must your audit trail have recorded?

choices.text: The final record pushed to the CRM plus the reviewer's name, since together they show who approved which values
Input ID and hash, model and prompt versions, output and checks, who reviewed what and when, what was sent
The application's stdout logs for every step, kept for seven days to keep storage costs down
The name of the reviewer who approved it, since they are accountable for the final values

questions.explanation: To explain a decision later you need the full chain: which exact input (a hash proves it's the same file), which model and prompt produced the output, what the checks said, who changed or approved what and when, and what left the system. Short-lived logs and the final record alone can't answer "why".

sources.title: Logging Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Each logged event should record when, where, who and what (timestamp, application, actor identity, event type and description), and logs should be protected with tamper detection and read-only storage.

questions.prompt: Why should the audit trail be append-only, and how would you store it?

model_answer.summary: Append-only means history can't be quietly rewritten, so the trail is trustworthy; store each step as an immutable event linked to the original document, and protect the documents themselves from changes.
key_points: Each step (received, extracted, validated, reviewed, pushed) is written as a new event with a timestamp and an actor, whether a model version or a person
Events are never updated or deleted; a correction is a new event that refers to the old one
Each event links to the source document by ID and content hash
Source documents are kept unchangeable, for example in S3 with versioning or Object Lock (write-once-read-many)
A retention period is defined to meet the business's or regulator's rules

questions.explanation: If records can be edited in place, the trail proves nothing. An event log also lets you replay what happened to one document. S3 Object Lock prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a fixed time or indefinitely, which is designed for exactly this kind of write-once requirement.

sources.title: Locking objects with Object Lock
sources.claim: S3 Object Lock uses a write-once-read-many model to stop object versions being deleted or overwritten for a fixed period or indefinitely (legal hold), and works only in buckets with S3 Versioning enabled.

sources.title: Logging Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Each logged event should record when, where, who and what (timestamp, application, actor identity, event type and description), and logs should be protected with tamper detection and read-only storage.
